How it works

A plain-language tour of the moving parts: what runs where, where your data sits, what protects it, and what an update actually does.

Two programs, two kinds of machine

  • The panel — the website you log into. It holds the user list, quotas, expiry dates, settings and the audit log.
  • OVNode — a small agent on every VPN server. It owns OpenVPN, the certificates and the per-user files.

The panel always calls the node. Nodes never call the panel — a node does not even store the panel's address — so you can move or replace the panel at any time without touching the VPN servers. Re-add them with the same address, name and API key and they carry on.

What runs where

On the panel

Two processes and one SQLite file. The web server serves requests and runs the live collector; a supervised child process runs the periodic jobs — traffic accounting, limit enforcement, backups, pruning and alerts — so a job that blocks cannot stop the panel answering. One service starts and stops both, and the child takes an exclusive lock on the data directory so a second one cannot start and double every schedule.

Neither process runs as root. A systemd unit starts them as ovmanager, a dedicated unprivileged account: the web server reads its own code, .env and the TLS key through that account's group, and owns the data directory. The panel is reachable from the network and parses untrusted input, so a compromise of the web app should not be a compromise of the host. The consequence is that the panel cannot replace its own code — that needs root — so the update button in the UI prints sudo ovm update instead. Docker runs the app as its own appuser for the same reason.

There is no external database, cache or message queue to run or keep alive. There is one SQLite database, and a configured Telegram bot runs as a supervised subprocess next to the two processes.

Why not Redis. A shared cache pays off when several application processes must share state. Here the web process is the only reader of the live cache and the periodic jobs coordinate through SQLite, which is already the source of truth — so a Redis hop would only add latency, a second thing to run and back up, and a few tens of megabytes of resident memory. It becomes worthwhile when the panel moves to multiple web workers, and that means replacing SQLite with a networked database first.

What the panel does instead of a cache tier:

  • One background collector polls the nodes and caches the result. Request handlers read that cache rather than fanning out to every node per request.
  • The collector backs off to OVMANAGER_LIVE_IDLE_POLL_SECONDS (default 300) when no browser has the live stream open, instead of probing every node every 10 seconds for an audience of nobody.
  • The built index.html is cached in memory and invalidated by mtime, so serving a dashboard route is one stat() rather than a file read per navigation.
  • Security-header and CSRF handling are plain ASGI middlewares, which keeps the live event stream unbuffered.

On a VPN node

  • The agent — a small web API listening on the service port (2083 by default).
  • OpenVPN — the daemon, run by systemd on a host install or supervised by the container entrypoint in Docker.
  • The hooks — small scripts under OpenVPN's ovnode/scripts/ that run at connect and disconnect time. That is where the login limit and the traffic counting actually happen.

There is no database on a node. Everything is plain files on disk.

How they talk

The panel connects out to each node and calls its /sync/... endpoints. Every request carries the node's API key in a key header, and every reply is the same small envelope: 

{"success": true, "msg": "...", "data": {...}}

The panel treats a call as successful only when it gets HTTP 200 and "success": true, so the node reports business failures inside the envelope rather than as an HTTP error.

TLS is verified strictly first. A node using a self-signed certificate — the installer default — fails that check, so the panel retries once without verification and warns loudly, once per node, as a standing reminder to move that node to Let's Encrypt. See TLS certificates.

Where the data lives

WhereWhat
/var/lib/ovmanager The panel's ovmanager.db: users, nodes, login sessions, settings and the audit log. WAL mode lets the jobs process write while you browse.
/opt/ovmanager The installed panel tree, with its own virtualenv and .env.
/etc/openvpn/ovnode/users/<cn>/ One folder per VPN user on a node: display name, login limit and disabled flag, and a cached .ovpn.
/etc/openvpn/server/ The node's OpenVPN configuration and PKI.
/var/lib/ovnode/<name>/ The node agent's own data, under the node's --name.

Node data survives a reinstall only if you keep the same node name: a different name reads a different, empty folder and orphans the old one.

Identity: one number per user

A user's numeric panel id is their OpenVPN common name: user 42 gets certificate CN 42. The node stores the display name beside it, so usage can be reported by username while the certificate layer stays numeric. Each user can carry an optional free-text tag of up to 64 characters (monthly, vip, reseller-a) that shows on the row and is searchable and filterable.

Traffic accounting and limits

Every five minutes the panel asks each node for its lifetime byte totals and bills only the increase, so a restart, a disconnect or a short session cannot double-count, and a total that shrinks — a rebuilt node — bills zero rather than a negative number. The full picture, including enforcement, is in Traffic limits.

The device limit is not policed from the panel. max_logins is pushed to every node and enforced by the connect hook: 1 means a new connection takes over the old one, N rejects the N+1th, and 0 is unlimited. Session identity is the CN plus the VPN pool address, which stays stable for the life of a session — so users whose real address changes on every reconnect are still counted and limited correctly. The panel only aggregates session counts, and can disconnect a user on any node.

Security model

  • Credentials live in the database, not in .env. The owner is an ordinary admins row; ADMIN_USERNAME in .env only says which row is the owner. Changing the owner password is ovm reset-password, and it rewrites that row. The panel ignores the older ADMIN_PASSWORD / ADMIN_PASSWORD_HASH lines and logs a warning when it sees them.
  • The trust boundary is the filesystem. Secrets in the database — node API keys, the Telegram bot token — are stored as written; there is no at-rest encryption, by design, because encrypting them would only move the key to another file on the same host. What protects them is the file modes, so those are load-bearing: the data and backup directories are 0700, and the database, the node certificates and every .ovmbak bundle are 0600. Treat an off-site backup as secret material and move it over an encrypted channel.
  • Secret URL path. The panel is served under a random prefix such as /k3f9xq2m/. Anything outside it gets an empty 404, so internet scanners see an empty site. It hides the panel; it is not login.
  • Database-backed sessions. A login returns an opaque random token and only its SHA-256 hash is stored. Sessions slide on activity and expire, logout deletes the row, and restarting the panel does not log everyone out. Failed logins are rate-limited per user and per address.
  • On the node the OpenVPN management interface listens on localhost only and requires a password file, because containers and host networking can share localhost. The PKI is ECDSA (prime256v1) with tls-crypt, a TLS 1.3 minimum, CRL enforcement and privilege dropping to an unprivileged runtime user. Client profiles embed the private key, so they are created owner-only and written atomically. A PKI failure starts the agent in diagnostics mode instead of killing it.

Updates

The installer does not build from source. It downloads a verified release archive and its mandatory SHA-256 sidecar and refuses to continue if the download is not a real archive or the checksum does not match.

sudo ovm update stages the new version, health-checks it, and restores the previous code if it does not answer. The database migrates itself on the next start. An update interrupted mid-flight by a power loss is cleaned up by sudo ovm recover-update, and the previous tree is available as sudo ovm rollback.

On a node, ovn update takes a verified snapshot of the identity file, the node data directory, /etc/openvpn and the API TLS files before it swaps in a release, and restores the snapshot if the new release does not come up healthy.

Backups

ovm backup writes a verified .ovmbak bundle of the panel database; ovn backup archives the node's data and PKI. Both keep the newest 14 by default and both have a daily systemd timer. Restoring an upload refuses writes with HTTP 503 until the swap finishes, keeps the replaced database as a fallback, and migrates the restored one on the spot. See Backups & restore.

The panel's container image

The Dockerfile is three stages, and the split is the point: the runtime image carries nothing a running panel does not need.

  1. frontend builds the dashboard. Node never reaches the runtime stage.
  2. builder installs the Python dependencies from a frozen lock, which fails closed if the lock and the project file have drifted apart. The compiler lives here and only here.
  3. runtime ships the virtualenv, the sources and the frontend build. No compiler, no build tooling.

It runs as a non-root appuser in the ovpanel group, which is what lets the container read the config bind-mounted at /app/.env. The installer refuses a group id that already has members on the host, because sharing that file by group would hand the secret panel URL path to them.

Schema migrations

The database is migrated automatically on every start. The current version is recorded in a schema_version table, so numbered steps run once and in order. Databases created by an earlier release are adopted: their current shape is inspected, missing columns are added, and the database is stamped at the current version — no dump and restore.

The design system

Every colour, space, radius, shadow and font in the dashboard comes from a design token, a CSS custom property declared in exactly one file, frontend/src/tokens.css. That file is the only place allowed to declare :root or html[data-theme=...], and the rule is enforced mechanically by npm run check:tokens, which fails the build if a token block appears anywhere else. The same script resolves the var() chain and asserts WCAG AA contrast for the text/background pairs that matter, in both themes.

Two consequences worth knowing if you are changing the dashboard:

  • Use semantic tokens, not hex. A component asks for var(--danger-text) or var(--space-3), never #e5484d. Both themes are then a palette swap in one file rather than a hunt through every stylesheet.
  • Both themes are declared side by side. Dark is the default :root; light is an override in the same file, so a new token that forgets one theme is visible in review rather than on someone's screen.
